reviewEvidence.visualReviewMethod: Six-second contact sheets across full duration; English burn-in and phase labels inspected; not continuous audio listening or all-frame review.
reviewEvidence.resolutionNote: Research-only reference media; never a production source. Independent production footage still requires genuine FHD or higher.

centralQuestion: Which functional stages make up an attack, and how do their poses and timings help a player read and control it?
thesis: Specify a stable starting pose, readable lead-in and impact pose, and expressive recovery; separate the visual return to idle from the moment control becomes available again.
titleCorrection: The source introduces FOUR elements including standby. The active motion has three stages, so a three-stage title must still teach the standby baseline.

claims: Introduce standby, lead-in, attack and follow-through as four elements.
Ground and aerial standby poses are the stable origins for most animations; settle these early.
sections.observedVisuals: Link on a grid runs the labeled phases; Link ground standby and Mario aerial standby are paired.
sections.ownScreenProposal: One own grid mannequin with persistent four-part timeline; distinguish base state from the three action stages.
sections.transitionToNext: From the baseline, the player first needs visible confirmation that an attack has started.

claims: Lead-in is anticipation or windup before attack.
The source's attacks often jump to a large pose change immediately rather than spending many frames smoothly leaving standby.
This shows input recognition promptly and gives the opponent an early signal to dodge.
sections.observedVisuals: Link lead-in on grid; Donkey Kong immediate body pose change; Fox/Falco illustrate opponent response.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Show input indicator and synchronized character views with immediate readable pose versus a delayed pose. All timings are our demonstration values.
sections.transitionToNext: The early signal leads to the decisive pose at which the attack can connect.

claims: The attack pose covers the time at or near hit registration.
Hit stop often emphasizes contact, making the visible impact pose especially important.
sections.observedVisuals: Link grid slash and actual Smash contact examples including Ganondorf/Luigi and a held collision moment.
sections.ownScreenProposal: On the same grid, activate our illustrative hit region at contact and hold the impact pose briefly; label hit stop without pretending the freeze is a measured commercial-game value.
prerequisites: Attack hit region versus body shape
Hit Stop: a brief contact pause, distinct from recovery
sections.transitionToNext: After contact stops registering, the body still has to complete its movement.

claims: Follow-through is the recovery interval after the active attack.
Use this interval to express what just happened instead of leaving the body nearly idle while input remains locked.
sections.observedVisuals: Link's full grid follow-through maintains a distinct stretched attack pose before returning.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Continue the same motion and time bar; compare a held meaningful silhouette with a bland near-idle recovery of the same duration.
sections.transitionToNext: The visible return and the point where the player can act need not occur at the same time.

claims: A cancel frame permits another action before the full animation visually returns to standby.
Move, jump or attack can therefore begin during the final recovery.
The source contrasts this with its implementation through Smash Melee, where waiting for full standby made control feel more rigid.
sections.observedVisuals: Grid labels cancel; Link interrupts into running and other moves; older Smash footage illustrates the historical contrast.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Place distinct markers for control-enabled and visual-idle on one timeline; trigger a queued jump at the first marker. Keep illustrative numbers separate from game facts.
prerequisites: Animation length versus control lock duration
Cancel here means opening an allowed action transition, not deleting an animation asset
sections.transitionToNext: These distinctions can be handed to animators as a compact set of concrete requirements.

claims: The briefing specifies standby pose, attack pose, attack-start frame and total frames until cancellation is allowed.
These anchors locate lead-in and follow-through and give animators a useful starting framework.
Specific art-direction feedback still complements the four fields.
sections.observedVisuals: Pose reference and Inkling spreadsheet highlight the four anchors; four-phase bar summarizes the relationship.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Fill four fields in our motion spec while the existing grid timeline updates. Use a small 60 fps numerical example and show frames/60 seconds conversion beside the relevant marker.
sections.transitionToNext: Conclude by replaying the fully labeled attack, now understandable as a chain rather than one opaque motion.

canonicalTerms.note: Visual follow-through and input lock are related but not identical.

omissionsAndReasons: Remove personal attribution and end teaser about future videos; preserve all four functional elements and the cancellation distinction.
Historical comparison is an implementation example, not a claim that every game before/after one release handles all cancel systems identically.
